extraction_notes.note: This paper has a retraction notice published July 5, 2006 (visible on each page of the PDF as a watermark/header: 'See Retraction Published July 5, 2006'). The data extracted here reflect the original 1998 publication content, not any retraction or correction. Systematic reviewers should verify the retraction notice and determine whether to include this study.

No numeric MNI or Talairach coordinates are reported anywhere in the paper. All neural activation results are described qualitatively (e.g., 'activation of occipital lobes') and shown in figures only. Coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis is not possible from this paper.
extraction_notes.source_location: Results section and all figures, pages 2671–2672

extraction_notes.note: No sensory or interoceptive outcome measures (deqi, VAS pain, tingling, etc.) were reported for any condition. This information was not assessed or collected according to the paper.
No expectancy, credibility, blinding success, or allocation guessing measures were reported.
No adverse events were reported or mentioned.
The number of subjects who underwent nonacupoint (control) stimulation is not specified; it is described only as a control condition with one representative volunteer shown (Volunteer 1 in Fig. 3).
extraction_notes.source_location: Methods and Results, page 2671; Fig. 3 caption, page 2671

extraction_notes.note: The paper states 'Among 12 volunteers, 8 were yang and 4 were yin.' However, Table 1 shows that the visual stimulation signal change values are all listed as positive (no minus sign for visual stimulation column), while acupuncture signal changes are listed as negative for 'yang' subjects. The sign convention for the '-' indicator in the volunteer column (e.g., '#1 (female, 21) -') refers to yang character, not a negative value for visual stimulation. This may cause confusion in interpreting Table 1.
extraction_notes.source_location: Table 1, page 2673; Methods and Results, page 2672

extraction_notes.note: The yin/yang classification is based on oriental medicine concepts and the paper does not provide a validated instrument or standardized criteria for classification. The blind test is described briefly with only one inconsistent case noted.
The paper does not specify which volunteers underwent VA2, VA3, and VA8 stimulation (Fig. 5 shows only Volunteer 3). It is unclear whether all 12 volunteers were tested with all four acupoints.
extraction_notes.source_location: Methods and Results, page 2671–2672; Fig. 5 caption, page 2672

extraction_notes.note: Flip angle is reported as 40 degrees. FOV is 220 mm. Slice thickness is 10 mm. Number of slices and matrix size are not reported.
No preprocessing details (motion correction parameters, normalization, smoothing, filtering) beyond positioning to avoid misregistration artifacts are reported.

The paradigm structure (number of on/off cycles, duration of each on and off block) beyond 'images 1–5 off, images 6–10 on' is not fully described. The repetition of this cycle is mentioned but the total number of cycles per run is not stated.

No statistical comparison between the visual stimulation and acupuncture stimulation conditions is reported (e.g., no t-test, no correlation between the two conditions). The claimed 'very close correlations' are based on qualitative visual comparison of activation maps and time-course plots.
extraction_notes.source_location: Abstract, page 2670; Methods and Results, page 2671

extraction_notes.note: The paper refers to 'flip angle of 40 degrees' and a TR of 60 ms with a CGE sequence. The very short TR (60 ms) is unusual for standard BOLD fMRI and may reflect a non-standard acquisition. The total acquisition time per image of 10 sec could mean a multi-slice acquisition. Extraction reflects the paper's reported values verbatim.
